summary: This informational document assesses the security of IETF IPv4 specifications and several mechanisms and policies in popular implementations. It is based on a project by the UK's Centre for the Protection of National Infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv4 was designed to share computers, not to survive an attacker, and the security notes were scattered across dozens of documents nobody could find. This RFC gathers them into one place, with a list of checks an implementation should make on every packet it receives.

subtitle: What the designers of IPv4 did not think about, and the checks a router or host should make on every packet it takes in.

tldr.problem: IPv4 was written to share computers, not to survive an attacker, and the security findings were scattered across dozens of documents that implementers could not easily find.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC goes through the header fields one at a time and the mechanisms the protocol implements, naming the threat in each and the check that would catch it.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It is a security roadmap for implementers, a set of sanity checks to apply before processing a packet, and a source of countermeasures for the fragmentation and address problems it finds.

today: RFC 6274 is an Informational document published in July 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an assessment rather than a specification: it lists the threats it found in IPv4 and the sanity checks it recommends, and leaves the fixes to implementers.

sections.title: Why This Assessment Exists
sections.content:
The TCP/IP protocols were conceived in an environment quite different from the hostile one they now operate in. Their effectiveness led to early adoption in production, to the point that the world's economy now depends on them to some extent. While many textbooks created the myth that the Internet protocols were designed for warfare, the top-level goal of the DARPA Internet Program was the sharing of large service machines on the ARPANET, so many protocol specifications focus only on the operational aspects and overlook their security implications.

The building blocks are still the same core protocols adopted more than two decades ago, and many vulnerabilities have been found in TCP/IP stacks since. Some came from flaws in particular implementations, affecting a reduced number of systems; others came from flaws in the protocols themselves, affecting virtually every implementation. Researchers were still working on core protocol security problems in the years just before this document was written.

When such vulnerabilities were found, reports came from several computer security incident response teams and vendors, which raised awareness but also scattered the documentation of protocol vulnerabilities across many documents that are sometimes hard to find. Much of the security community's work did not result in RFCs, so known problems were not always addressed by all vendors, and vendors often implemented quick fixes without a careful analysis of their effectiveness and their effect on interoperability. The lack of adoption by the IETF means that any system built to the official specifications today would reinvent security flaws that have already hit the network in the past.

Producing a secure TCP/IP implementation is now hard, in part because there is no single document serving as a security roadmap: implementers must find the relevant documentation and tell correct advice from misleading advice built on wrong assumptions. This document is the companion the RFCs lacked. It assesses the IETF specifications of IPv4 from a security point of view, identifies the threats, proposes countermeasures where possible, and also assesses the implementation strategies commonly found in the real world. It is heavily based on a security assessment of the Internet Protocol published by the UK's Centre for the Protection of National Infrastructure in 2008.

The scope is the specifications of IP itself; routing and bootstrapping protocols were out of scope. The primary sources were RFC 791 on the protocol itself, RFC 815 on datagram reassembly, RFC 919 on broadcasting, RFC 950 on subnetting, RFC 1112 on host extensions for multicasting, RFC 1122 on host requirements, RFC 1812 on router requirements, RFC 2474 and RFC 2475 on differentiated services, RFC 3168 on explicit congestion notification, and RFC 4632 on address assignment and aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 was designed to share computers, not to survive an attacker, and the security notes were scattered across dozens of documents nobody could find. This RFC gathers them into one place, with a list of checks an implementation should make on every packet it receives.

sections.title: The Header Fields and Their Checks
sections.content:
The document is in two parts: the header fields, one at a time, and the mechanisms the protocol implements. This section covers the header fields and the sanity checks the RFC says should be made before any processing of the header.

The size check. The minimum header is 20 bytes, but an IP module may be handed a datagram shorter than that, so the check is that the payload size handed up by the link layer is at least 20. If it fails, the packet should be dropped and the event logged.

Version. A four-bit field that must be 4 for IPv4. In practice different versions of IP are told apart by the link-layer protocol type, so a packet arriving with the wrong version should be silently dropped and logged; without that check an attacker could change the version field to confuse a sensor that picks its pattern-matching rules by version. A node should also check that IPv4 packets are handed to the IPv4 module when the link layer used the IPv4 protocol type, because an attacker could encapsulate IPv4 in another protocol type to subvert link-layer access control lists or tampering with sensors.

Header length. The IHL field gives the header length in four-byte words, so the minimum legal value is 5, and the header cannot be larger than the datagram, which gives two checks: IHL at least 5, and IHL times 4 no greater than the total length.

Type of service. The field has been reinterpreted twice: the original layout had precedence and delay, throughput, reliability and cost bits, which is still assumed by some deployed systems; RFC 2474 replaced it with a Differentiated Services code point plus a currently unused field, which RFC 3168 then turned into the Explicit Congestion Notification field. Because the code point decides how a packet is treated, an attacker could forge one to steal service or cause a denial of service: a codepoint of the form 11x000 gives preferential forwarding, and under strict priority queuing a continuous stream of such packets could starve flows with a lower relative order. Networks using the older semantics should remark the field at their boundary. On ECN, the RFC says the threat most easily exploited is a host falsely claiming to be ECN-capable: an attacker setting the ECT codepoint gets its packets marked rather than dropped during moderate congestion, while competing packets without the codepoint are dropped, so the attacker gets better service.

Total length. A 16-bit field covering the header and payload, so up to 65535 bytes, with hosts expected to handle at least 576. The module can be handed a packet larger than the total length, which is usually link-layer padding but could be malicious, so the buffer should be sized on what the link layer reports rather than on the total length field. The reverse can also happen, and could leak information, so the check is that the payload size handed up is at least the total length.

Identification and flags. The identification field is set by the sender to help reassembly, and needs to be unique at any time for each combination of source address, destination address and protocol. Many systems set it on a protocol-independent basis and simply increment it, which wraps more often than necessary and opens the door to information leakage: the field can be used to work out a system's packet rate, to conduct a stealth port scan through a third host, to uncover the rules of a number of firewalls, and to count the systems behind a NAT. Some operating systems set it to zero on packets with the Don't Fragment bit, but non-compliant middle boxes that fragment such packets would then produce collisions; Linux and Solaris later set it per IP address, which removes some of the problems but not all, since systems behind a load balancer can still be counted.

The three control bits are reserved, Don't Fragment and More Fragments. The Don't Fragment bit is usually set to implement path MTU discovery, but an attacker can also use it to evade a sensor: a large packet with the bit set is dropped by an intervening router that cannot forward it without fragmenting, and the sensor never learns that the packet never arrived. Some firewalls drop packets with both the More Fragments and Don't Fragment bits set, which can happen legitimately when a middle box fragments a too-large packet and copies the bit, or on Linux, which sets both bits to implement path MTU discovery for UDP.

Fragment offset. It says where in the original payload the fragment belongs, in units of eight bytes, so all fragments except the last must be aligned on an eight-byte boundary, and the check is that the payload length minus the header length is a multiple of eight when the More Fragments bit is set. The field is 13 bits, so a fragment can claim to belong to a datagram larger than the 65535-byte maximum, and the RFC gives the check that catches it. In the worst case an attacker could craft fragments that reassemble into a datagram of 131043 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of this section is a list of checks a router should make before it looks at anything else in a packet: is it long enough, does it say the right version, does the header length make sense, are the fragments lined up. Each one closes a hole that attackers have used.

sections.title: The TTL Field: Fingerprinting and Defence
sections.content:
The time to live field bounds the lifetime of the packets inside it and stops packets looping for ever. It was originally meant to be a time in seconds, but because every module that handles a datagram must decrement it by at least one, it became a hop count in practice. Most systems let the administrator configure the value they originate, with the default usually a power of two or 255; the recommended value from IANA is 64, which reflects the assumed diameter of the Internet plus a margin.

Because the defaults are powers of two or 255, a packet that arrives with a TTL of 60 was probably sent with 64, and one that arrives with 120 was probably sent with 128, unless a protocol scrubber or transparent proxy has overwritten the field. Working out the original TTL is useful for fingerprinting the originating operating system, though since most systems share only a handful of defaults the granularity is negligible; for fingerprinting the physical device, counting the systems behind a NAT or a load balancer, since devices with different defaults or different distances would answer with different TTLs; for mapping the network topology, by raising the TTL a step at a time to elicit errors from the routers, which is what traceroute does; and for locating the source host in the topology, by comparing the TTLs seen at several cooperating hosts to work out how many hops away the sender is.

It can also be used to evade network intrusion detection systems. A sensor placed before the destination may see a packet that will never arrive, so the sensor's picture differs from the destination's. A general countermeasure is to normalize traffic at the edge of the organisation, and OpenBSD Packet Filter is an example of a packet filter with TTL normalization.

And it can be used defensively. Two directly connected peers can agree to require a TTL of 255 in every packet, because packets that crossed a router arrive with a smaller value, so only hosts on the same link can pass the check; that cuts the set of systems able to attack the application, and the same check is applied to the related ICMP error messages. For peers that are not directly connected, the check becomes TTL at least 255 minus the number of hops between them, which accepts packets from a smaller set of hosts. The IETF has documented this officially as the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism.

Two cautions go with it. A protocol scrubber that enforces a minimum TTL may help an attacker, by raising the TTL of the attacker's packets above what the check expects. And the originating host can set the TTL to a small value, often 1 for link-scope services, to limit how far the packet may travel.
sections.plainLanguage: The TTL counts hops. Because the starting value is usually a round number, an observer can guess it, and use it to fingerprint the sending system, count machines behind a NAT, or trace the route. The same field also lets two peers on the same link insist on a TTL of 255, which excludes everyone else.

sections.title: Fragment Reassembly and Its Problems
sections.content:
IP offers fragmentation by hosts and routers so that packets can cross networks with different maximum transmission units, and reassembly is done only by the end systems. Over the decades this has been exploited to evade sensors, bypass firewall rules and mount denial-of-service attacks.

The problem is the complexity of the function. Reassembly is a stateful operation inside a stateless protocol, so the receiving host must allocate memory both to hold the fragments and to do the reassembly, and an attacker can exhaust those buffers. The mechanism was designed when available bandwidth was very different from today's, so interoperability problems arise that attackers can exploit deliberately. Reassembly usually happens without any knowledge of the path the fragments took, so a host cannot make an educated guess about how long to wait for a missing fragment. The algorithm as specified is ambiguous and allows several interpretations, each found in different stacks. And the process itself is complex, because fragments may arrive out of order, duplicated or overlapping, and that complexity has produced many bugs.

On memory specifically, an attacker can send many forged fragments with different identification values and never send the fragments needed to complete them. Each one ties up resources until the reassembly timer expires. Some implementations make it worse by allocating a buffer big enough for the whole datagram as soon as any fragment arrives, so a single small fragment can tie up memory for the size of an extremely large datagram; the strategy suggested in RFC 815 leads to that. Whether the attack succeeds depends on the implementation: with no limit on the IP module's memory, the whole system can be tied up and may crash; with a limit on the module as a whole, all further IP packets are discarded until fragments time out; with a limit on fragment reassembly memory, further fragments are discarded until one times out.

The length of the identification field is part of the problem too, since it is only 16 bits, so it wraps quickly and the same identification value can be reused. The RFC's suggested remedies include allocating reassembly memory on the basis of what has actually been received rather than the claimed total length, flushing the fragment buffer, and reducing the reassembly timeout: RFC 791 said to wait at least 15 seconds, and the example procedure in that document could leave a timer running for up to 4.25 minutes, while RFC 1122 corrected this to a fixed value between 60 and 120 seconds. Shortening the timeout reduces how long resources stay tied up, at the cost of dropping legitimate datagrams whose fragments arrive slowly.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting a packet back together is the most complicated thing IPv4 does, and it is where most of the historic attacks live. A host has to hold memory for fragments that may never all arrive, and the time it waits for them is long enough for an attacker to fill the machine up.

sections.title: Addresses and Source Address Forgery
sections.content:
The source address of an IP datagram identifies the node the packet came from, and strictly speaking the interface it left from rather than the system. It is trivial to forge because of the apparent lack of consistent filtering near the edge of the network, and that has been used for denial-of-service attacks and for impersonating other systems where authentication relied on the source address alone. The extent of the problem can be reduced by ingress and egress filtering in the routers, and the RFC points to the existing guidance and to measurements of how susceptible the Internet is to forged source addresses. Checks should also be made on the addresses that appear elsewhere, such as those inside the payload of ICMP error messages. One of the RFC's plainest statements is that authentication should never rely solely on the source address.

The addressing section collects the checks that should be made on both address fields. Some addresses are meant to be unreachable from the public Internet, such as the private addresses and the loopback address, but an attacker can reach them by tricks such as the loose and strict source route options, so where applicable the filtering should be at the private network boundary. Link-local unicast addresses and multicast addresses of limited scope should not be reachable from outside their proper boundaries either.

Three blocks are reserved for private internets: 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255, 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 and 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255, and filtering at the organisational perimeter should make sure they are not reachable from outside. A packet received with an address from the former Class D block, the 224/4 block used for Internet multicast, as its source address should be dropped and logged. The former Class E addresses, the 240/4 block, are reserved for experimental use and most routers already discard them, so a packet with one as source or destination should be dropped and logged too. And because connection-oriented protocols such as TCP keep shared state between only two endpoints, a packet with a multicast or broadcast destination arriving for a connection-oriented protocol should be dropped and logged.
sections.plainLanguage: The source address on a packet can be forged almost anywhere, so it must never be used as proof of identity. The RFC also lists the addresses that a router should simply refuse: the private ranges, the old multicast range, and the old experimental range.

sections.title: What the Assessment Concludes
sections.content:
The document says it is not the final word on the security of the Internet Protocol. It aims to raise awareness of the many threats based on IP that have been faced in the past, are being faced now, or may still have to be dealt with in the future. It gives advice for a secure implementation and offers insights into the security aspects of IP that may help the operations community. Feedback from the community is encouraged, to keep the document accurate and up to date as new threats are found.

Two practical threads run through it. The first is that many vulnerabilities came from the protocol itself rather than from an implementation, which is why the checks are set out as rules for the header rather than left to each vendor. The second is the packet-of-death class of attack, where a single specially crafted packet crashes the IP implementation or makes it misbehave: in most cases the attack packet is simply malformed, and in other cases it is well formed but exercises a little-used path through the stack. Well-designed implementations should protect against these, and the RFC describes the sanity checks expected to prevent most of those vectors. Where an implementation is found to be vulnerable, the RFC says administrators have to fall back on mitigating them with packet filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not claim to have the last word. It is a checklist for implementers and a reference for anyone auditing a network, and it asks to be told about new problems as they turn up.

viz.caption: THE IPV4 HEADER, FROM FIGURE 1 OF RFC 6274

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Must be 4 for IPv4; a packet with another value should be dropped.

fields.name: IHL
fields.desc: Header length in 32-bit words. Must be at least 5.

fields.name: Type of Service
fields.desc: Now the Differentiated Services code point plus the ECN field.

fields.name: Total Length
fields.desc: Length of the header and payload in bytes, up to 65535.

fields.name: Identification
fields.desc: Set by the sender to help reassemble fragments.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved, Don't Fragment and More Fragments.

fields.name: Fragment Offset
fields.desc: Where the fragment belongs in the original payload, in units of eight bytes.

fields.name: Time to Live
fields.desc: Hop count; decremented by every module that forwards the packet.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: The protocol encapsulated in the datagram.

fields.name: Source Address
fields.desc: The interface the packet came from. It can be forged.

fields.name: Destination Address
fields.desc: The interface the packet is meant for.

viz.caption: WHAT THE TTL FIELD CAN BE USED FOR

items.title: OS fingerprinting
items.text: The default TTL differs between operating systems, so the original value narrows the guess.

items.title: Device fingerprinting
items.text: Different TTLs arriving from behind a NAT suggest different devices behind it.

items.title: Mapping the topology
items.text: Raising the TTL a step at a time is how traceroute finds the routers on the path.

items.title: Locating the source
items.text: Cooperating hosts can compare TTLs to work out how many hops away the sender is.

items.title: Evading a sensor
items.text: A sensor placed before the destination may see a packet that never arrives.

items.title: GTSM as a defence
items.text: Requiring a TTL of 255 between peers on the same link cuts the set of hosts that can attack.

viz.caption: WHY FRAGMENT REASSEMBLY IS HARD TO GET RIGHT

cells: The host must hold memory for fragments that may never complete
The host cannot guess how long to wait for a missing fragment
Different stacks interpret the same fragments in different ways
Fragments arrive out of order, duplicated and overlapping, which has produced many bugs
RFC 1122 puts it at 60 to 120 seconds, tying up memory for that long
